item.title: Do readers really want books by committee?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Do readers really want books by committee?

A new imprint from Harper Voyager is betting they do.

As reported by Maia Snow in The Bookseller, Between Worlds is a new community-oriented imprint that “will publish fantasy, romantasy, dark academia, horror and dystopia as well as requests from members of the community.”

The new imprint was announced via an unboxing video on Instagram, with a caption explaining that Between Worlds “will be kind of like a book club! They will ask readers about their opinions and feedback! So for example, you have a say in what they publish and can even share which designs you prefer and what merch they bring out! ⭐️” All of the imprint’s decisions, from editorial through marketing, will be informed by reader choices, it seems.

Between Worlds’s own Instagram foregrounds the book club part of the project (“A fantasy community and imprint”) and describes their process, which will “use surveys, polls and community discussions to find out what you would like to read … and what you’re tired of! We then find those stories and work with amazing author, illustrators, designers, and booksellers to bring you your next reading obsession.” Community management will flow up through all parts of the process. Whether this works to produce sales or good books remains to be seen, but combining a membership model with publishing is probably a savvy way to boost sales, or at least guarantee a dependable floor on sales figures.

Between Worlds sounds similar to Bindery Books, which is also built around a full integration of members and influencers into the work of publishing. Bindery’s app caters to influencers, folding in affiliate sales and revenue sharing, along with the offer of a co-produced imprint: “Tastemakers with thriving communities have the opportunity to launch a branded imprint fully supported by Bindery’s in-house publishing team.”

I’m not the target audience here, but I don’t recognize any of Bindery’s titles. But I do recognize the types of titles they’re putting out. The vibe of a romantasy cover or a thriller cover is immediately legible: if this is the type of book you read, the cover says, here is another like it.

Again, this is probably a good sales tactic, and I’m not saying I’m above this sort of recognizable marketing. When I spot a book cover with an old painting and the title and author in a solid pastel box, I’m thinking “NYRB” and checking it out. And did I think about dressing as a Fitzcarraldo Edition for Halloween but couldn’t find the right shade of blue clothes? Ask me next October.

But directly integrating this kind of marketing branding into the editorial process strikes me as risky, and pushing things towards a hazy, bland median. And I imagine it will create a feedback loop that will drive their output in one direction. (That so much culture is feeling more generic isn’t just the fault of creative production underestimating audiences taste or capability to handle challenge—it also comes down, at least partially, to the audience itself.) Plus, the shift towards “you sell yourself a book” is another blow for the self-checkout-ification of industries, where labor downsizing and the offloading of work onto the consumer is packaged as choice and community.

I know I’m being naive about how creative decisions have long been made. I know that focus groups are nothing new. And Lord knows I spent enough years as an improvisor to know that art by committee can be great. But I also know that a majority of improv shows aren’t good—they’re bad, even—and that something profound or moving coming out of design by committee is rare. For every story like the movie Airplane! being sharpened by test audience reactions, there are many more Poochies and Europa Jeeps.

With books, giving readers the keys to acquiring new voices and new stories seems ironically risky to me, even though it’s likely motivated by a desire to hedge on editorial risk. A traditional editorial process doesn’t guarantee good books or bestsellers either, but asking a book club to prompt their dream novel introduces more questions for me: How do you maintain variety and diversity? How do you keep things from getting boring? And how will you find a book that will be genuinely surprising?

A memorable book is often the one that you didn’t expect—I’ve rarely been bowled over by something that delivered exactly on my expectations. Maybe these focus-grouped books, that are delivering on a set of wishes and packaged to look like the kind of book you already read, aren’t actually meant to be memorable or challenging books. Maybe they don’t need to be, and only have to exist within the continuum of a reader’s stated taste and preference. I see the logic in making the “customers also bought” section of every webstore into an editorial mission statement. But while not everything needs to be a transcendent experience, why not dream a little, and put resources towards those higher aspirations?

Cover image from @betweenworldsbookclub on Instagram

James Folta

James Folta is a staff writer at Lit Hub and the managing editor of Points in Case. He co-writes the weekly Newsletter of Humorous Writing. More at www.jamesfolta.com, or you can reach me at jfolta@lithub.com.

Check Out NPR’s Interactive Guide to the Best Books of 2026

NPR has dropped their interactive guide to 389 of the best books of 2026, as selected by both NPR staffers and trusted critics across the book world.

NPR’s Books We Love 2026 list is broken down into dozens of categories, inviting users to peruse picks based on the topics, genres, or categories they’re interested in. You can dive into NPR Staff picks, as well as great picks for book clubs. There are options to check out the best of debuts, romance, nonfiction, and more. The ability to drill down across multiple categories makes finding “best of” picks with more highly specific interests is possible: you can mix-and-match seriously great writing with rather short, for example.

Because the list is so expansive, there are books among the “best of” picks that other outlets could not include due to space or may have simply missed.

Among some of NPR’s Books We Love picks are:

- John of John by Douglas Stuart

- As You Wake, Break the Shell by Becky Chambers

item.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Nonfiction Books of 2026
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Reading Lists

Electric Lit’s Top 10 Nonfiction Books of 2026

Books by Camonghne Felix, Joseph Osmundson, and Franny Choi are among our favorites of the year

This article is free to read. So is every article Electric Literature publishes. No limits, no paywalls—now or ever. Support from readers like you makes that possible.

We need to raise $60,000 to start off 2027 strong. Donate now to our end of year fundraiser to help ensure the future of free, accessible literature for all.

—————

This year, I read more nonfiction books than ever before. It wasn’t planned, though I suppose it had something to do with wanting to understand a world that seems increasingly fractured and confounding. For years, one political crisis has given way to another, each arriving with its own predictions of what terrible thing awaits us next. Reading nonfiction offered a way of making sense of it all, beyond the endless stream of news on my screen.

Curiously, the books that helped me best think about the future were often concerned with the past. In Turn (W)here, Chet’la Sebree reckons with America’s history of racism as she considers what it would mean to raise a Black child in a country still shaped by that history. The past can make the future feel all too predictable. These days, it’s hard not to imagine what’s coming in dystopian terms, from climate catastrophe to forever wars to—new fear unlocked—AI-driven human extinction.

And yet, history has a way of defying our expectations. The recent victories of the political left in this year’s midterm elections felt like a fulcrum—the whole country tilted blue and another future became imaginable. Of course, I am wary of getting carried away by optimism; the past is full of futures that never arrived. In An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail, Hélène Giannecchini recovers forgotten forms of intimacy and solidarity through the stories of queer people whose lives and ways of living have been largely overlooked.

If the past is riddled with unrealized possibilities, perhaps the task is not simply to recover them, but to imagine new ones. I ended the year reading Camonghne Felix’s Let the Poets Govern, which draws on Black radical poetic traditions to imagine new forms of collective life. And while there’s no telling what the future might bring, this year’s crop of our top nonfiction books reminded me that the catastrophes we’re warned about, however real their threats, are not the only futures available to us. It is precisely this uncertainty that makes hope possible.

Here are our favorite nonfiction books of 2026.

–Evander James Reyes

Communications Manager

Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. Books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration. The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked.

An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail by Hélène Giannecchini, translated by Anna Moschovakis

In An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail, Hélène Giannecchini follows queer relationships that taught her a history her family could not pass down: friends, lovers, mentors, and strangers whose lives survive in photographs, diaries, and remembered gestures. Moving from Casa Susanna to Donna Gottschalk’s images and a record of a French man living with HIV, the book asks how people find one another across time. Giannecchini approaches research as an intimate encounter, letting uncertainty and the desire to locate herself among these lives guide what she discovers. You can read an excerpt of the book here, which is also the first translation published in EL’s Personal Narrative! It is a fitting place to begin: a hybrid work about how one life opens onto many others.

–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Feels Like Trouble by Helen Betya Rubinstein

By expertly weaving personal narrative with much-needed critique on academia and craft, Helen Betya Rubinstein has created a delightfully probing and compulsively readable collection of essays or, as the title (quite accurately) calls them, “provocations.” Feels Like Trouble takes a scalpel to the writing life, laying bare the problems at the center of how we teach and talk about what makes writing “good.” This book is a salve for anyone who’s been unmoored from their artistic instincts by instruction that harmed more than it helped. It’s also an instructive call to action for how we might rethink the status quo. Rubinstein may have experienced teachers who tried to quash her voice along the way, but in this book, it’s on full display: sharp, rebellious, and clear-eyed. Read an excerpt of the book in EL’s personal narrative.

–Katie Henken Robinson, Deputy Editor

The Flower Bearers by Rachel Eliza Griffiths

In The Flower Bearers, Rachel Eliza Griffiths navigates a season of devastating rupture: the sudden death of her closest friend, poet Kamilah Aisha Moon, followed swiftly by the public stabbing of her husband, Salman Rushdie. Through the catastrophe, Griffiths grounds her story in the sanctuary of Black literary circles and the lifelong practice of making art, framing this memoir as a profound mediation on witness. Moving from alienated graduate workshops to hospital bedside vigils, Griffiths shows that carrying love through grief requires stubborn, daily attention. She tenders a rare, vivid record of how we rebuild ourselves in the company of what survives.

–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Let the Poets Govern by Camonghne Felix…

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

The Best Books of 2026, BIPOC Edition

‘Tis the season of Best-Of lists, and just last week we released the list of our favorite books of the year. Our staff and contributors read widely, so the list is a great mix of different genres and age categories, and includes fiction and nonfiction alike.

Among our favorites were many books by BIPOC authors. In the 29 books below, you’ll find the latest by heavy hitters like Tayari Jones, Marlon James, and Elizabeth Acevedo, as well as unsettling short stories, a mystery-bildungsroman blend, romance, and lots more.

Anger Is Only a Shadow by Elizabeth Acevedo

Elizabeth Acevedo began her publishing career exceptionally with The Poet X, and has remained nothing short of a gifted writer. Acevedo once again delivers a powerful story, this time through the eyes of Lil, following a quick stint in juvie and now under probation with an ankle monitor. Watching her navigate family, school, and her brother’s mental health crisis, all in a world where the systems are designed against her— as her impulsive nature always picks the wrong path—will have you rooting so hard for her and ready to fight anyone who isn’t. And as always, Acevedo’s audiobook narration is all-the-awards-worthy. —Jamie Canaves

Bad Words by Rioghnach Robinson

Novelist Parker Navarro was supposed to be a star, until literary critic Selina Chan gave his debut a scathing review—and her review of his sophomore novel is just as brutal as the first. When Parker confronts Selina at an event, it’s caught on video and goes viral. Overnight, they find themselves in a true literary feud. They begin to exchange snarky emails that expand into something like friendship. Meanwhile, the literary world is obsessed with their feud. As the pair navigate social media, complex family dynamics, and the pressures of fame, they find connection. The slowest of slow burns, this enemies-to-lovers romance feels real. —Courtney Rodgers

Cleopatra by Saara El-Arifi

Weaving history and fantasy together, this retelling of Cleopatra imagines the pharaoh’s story in her own voice. The truth is, we know very little of the real Cleopatra VII, and most of what has been told is through the perspective of the Roman Empire. Because of that, Cleopatra has been called a witch, a whore, even a villain. She’s thought of as the woman who “ended” Egypt’s reign. But thanks to Saara El-Arifi, we can now imagine what her actual life (and not only her death) was like in this gorgeous character study. —Rey Rowland

Encore!: A Graphic Novel by Miles Toriko Burks

2026 has been my year of being obsessed with Heartstopper, and as such, I read a lot of books this year that claimed to be for fans of the series. Encore! is one of the very few that lives up to the comparison. First of all, the art is gorgeous. The second-chance romance is also very sweet: Clay and Aron used to be best friends, until they had a falling out. When they are paired up in a theater class, old feelings come to the surface. This is definitely one for the queer theater kids, and I loved the supportive friend group that rounds out the cast. If you need a pick-me-up, add this YA graphic novel romance to your TBR. —Danika Ellis

Good People by Patmeena Sabit

This book has haunted me all year! It’s a searing crime drama about an immigrant family, the Sharafs, told through interview transcripts. The Sharafs came to the U.S. many years ago and have been seemingly living the American dream. They have children with great prospects, excellent jobs, money, a big house, and fancy cars. But when one of the Sharafs dies unexpectedly, the rumors and stories start to come out. What really happened? And is it jealously, disapproval, or racism behind the growing stories about the Sharafs and their lives? This incredible debut offers many possibilities but ultimately makes you search yourself for the answers. —Liberty Hardy

Kin by Tayari Jones

Jones’s newest was an instant success, selected for Oprah’s Book Club before rocketing up the bestseller list and winning a Kirkus Prize. Her historical fiction follows two young Black women, cradle friends with tragic and complicated family histories, whose paths diverge. The contrast between Vernice’s journey into an HBCU and affluent circles and Annie’s hardscrabble quest to find her estranged mother exemplifies how different and yet alike the experience of being a Black woman coming of age in the American South can look. This story is a powerful study of a point in history where Black Americans strove for success while Jim Crow tried to beat them down. —S. Zainab Williams

Let the Poets Govern by Camonghne Felix

At a time of extreme political pessimism and despondence, Camonghne Felix’s Let the Poets Govern is exactly the book we all need. Felix, a phenomenal poet and a political speechwriter and strategist, considers the power of poetry in politics—as well as the inherent role of politics in poetry. Words have immense power, and when they’re used beautifully, creatively, and intentionally, they can heal something in our broken world. Felix uses a combination of prose, poetry, and experimental forms to showcase the power poetry has to save our democracy and our humanity. —Susie Dumond

Mazywood by Tananarive Due

The Queen of Black Horror has a brilliant way of weaving real-life horrors into her novels, and Mazywood is no exception. This time, it’s the 1920s when a young Mazelle Washington wishes for a friend and gets a swampy dog with whom she has a unique connection. Meanwhile, in the present day, we find Mazy’s grandson, filmmaker Johnny Washington, has just moved his family to his grandmother’s mountain retreat, aptly called “Mazywood.” He’s still contending with his grandmother’s Hollywood legacy as one of the few Black actresses, but there are also Mazy’s secrets…one of which involves the big, strange thing skulking just out of sight. —Erica Ezeifedi

My Dear You by Rachel Khong…

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Best Mystery and Thriller Books of the Year

It’s a great way to discover new titles that you may have missed along the way. I’m thrilled to be able to share some of my picks for the best mystery and thriller books of the year along with fellow Rioters’ picks for the year, too. These include a murder mystery based on a 19th-century classic, the latest release in a paranormal mystery series, a literary mystery set at a Pacific Northwest boarding school, and more.

If you want more best books of the year, check out Book Riot’s full Best Books of 2026 list.

My 3 Favorite Mystery and Thriller Books of 2026

Beth is Dead by Katie Bernet

When I first heard the book idea, a Little Women murder mystery, I’ll admit I was a bit skeptical. Thanks to another mystery writer’s assurances, I decided to check it out and boy, he was right. When Rob March wrote a book about his four daughters, it changed the March family’s lives forever. Now everyone knows their names and their life story without their consent. Worse yet, he decided to have Beth die in the book, even though Beth is very much alive. Until her body is found in the woods. Now everyone is a suspect in the murder of Beth March, including her three sisters. It’s an amazing adaptation of the 19th-century classic in a 21st-century mystery context.

Tata by Valérie Perrin, Translated by Hildegarde Serle

This book is more of a mystery than a murder mystery, but it’s definitely a journey well worth taking. Finally translated into English, Tata begins with the most intriguing premise: One day, Agnes gets a phone call that her Aunt Colette “Tata” had died. But Agnes buried her aunt three years prior. Agnes returns to her aunt’s village and investigates her aunt’s life to better understand how her aunt could possibly die twice. Despite its length (clocking in at 592 pages), you will feel compelled to read it in a single night.

The Key to a Killer by Olivia Blacke

A New Lease on Death was one of my favorite books of 2024. So I was very excited to see the stunning third book in the Ruby and Cordelia Mystery Series. And boy, it delivers. Ruby and Cordelia are not your typical roommates; mostly because Cordelia is dead and Ruby lives in her apartment. But they’ve joined forces, with some difficulty, to solve the murder of their neighbor and later a delivery driver. Now they’re tackling the hardest case yet: Cordelia’s death. And it sticks the landing

3 of Book Rioters’ Best Mystery and Thriller Books of 2026

I love how the genre spans so many subgenres, from horror, comedy, and even literary adaptations. I’m thrilled to learn about these new mystery and thriller books from my fellow writers at Book Riot. Enjoy!

Whidbey by T. Kira Madden

T Kira Madden’s novel, a literary mystery that faces down sexual assault and pedophilia with eyes wide open, is an astonishing debut. Guided by personal experience and a determination to do right by victims of sexual violence, the author of the memoir Long Live the Tribe of Fatherless Girls breathes life into victims, allies, abusers, and enablers through well-developed characters, none of whom smack of trope or stereotype. This emotionally charged read is as bracing as it is compelling, and it deserves more attention. —Sharifah Williams

Night Objects by Eli Raphael

In this mystery and coming-of-age novel, a young woman and her family have just moved from Miami to Washington State when her mother dies in a tragic accident. The girl is sent to a swanky boarding school that’s as steeped in privilege as it is in secrets, and she’s quickly recruited into a secret society that turns out to be a cult—and then there’s a murder. The general shape of this narrative is a familiar one, but Eli Raphael’s debut is at once a compelling mystery and brilliant work of literary fiction that examines privilege, race, class, identity, and grief. This debut snuck up on me this year, and I hope more people will read it. —Vanessa Diaz

The Sleeping Sisters by Jennifer Givhan

First, look at that gorgeous cover! Now onto the inside of the book. I’ve loved all of Jennifer Givhan’s crime books, which manage to keep getting better as she wraps a mystery around an interrogation of femicide, history, the lived experiences of women, generational trauma, folklore, and culture. After winning the lottery and moving her family to a wealthier neighborhood, Fortuna Miércoles finds her life, and mind, deteriorating thanks to a murder suspiciously similar to a serial killer’s crimes. As Detective Jeanette Palacio investigates, Fortuna finds herself unable to trust her mind, her new neighbors, and the men in her life. —Jamie Canaves

Those are our picks for six of the best mystery and thriller books of 2026. I hope that you add a few more books to your TBR! If you want some more recommendations, check out our mid-year list of the best mysteries, thrillers, and true crime, and brush up on the best mystery and thriller books of 2025.

Jefferson Airplane's Jorma Kaukonen says guitar has always been a 'great refuge'

Kaukonen helped define the sound of the '60s as the lead guitar player and a founding member of Jefferson Airplane. Now 85, he's still touring with his band Hot Tuna.

TERRY GROSS, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. Our guest, Jorma Kaukonen, was the lead guitar player and a founding member of Jefferson Airplane, one of the bands that defined psychedelic rock of the 1960s and served as the soundtrack for San Francisco's Summer of Love. Jorma's also had a long career with his other very popular band, Hot Tuna, which he still tours with. He spoke with FRESH AIR's executive producer, Sam Briger, about his life and career. Here's Sam.

SAM BRIGER, BYLINE: If you've ever heard the song "Somebody To Love" or "White Rabbit" by Jefferson Airplane, you've heard Jorma Kaukonen play electric guitar. But Jorma's one of those rare musicians with a compelling style on both acoustic and electric guitars. He's known as a terrific fingerstyle guitarist, deeply influenced by the music of Reverend Gary Davis, a blues and gospel musician who had a resurgence during the 1960s folk scene. Jorma was a Bay Area folky back then, meeting other like-minded musicians who would go on to acclaim as rock and roll phenoms - Jerry Garcia, his soon-to-be band member Paul Kantner and Janis Joplin - who he would accompany at local hootenannies.

Jorma left Jefferson Airplane in the early '70s to concentrate on his other band, Hot Tuna, and other solo projects. His 1974 album "Quah" is one of my favorite albums. He wrote a great memoir published in 2018 called "Been So Long," which details his tumultuous family upbringing, his life as a rock star and recovery from alcohol and drug addictions. At 85, he's still on the road playing gigs with Hot Tuna and as a solo act.

His most recent release is an archival live recording called "Wabash Avenue" from 1965, shortly before he co-founded Jefferson Airplane. One of the tracks on it is an early version of his song "Embryonic Journey," an acoustic instrumental, which would find its way onto Jefferson Airplane's second and most influential album, "Surrealistic Pillow." Let's listen.

(SOUNDBITE OF JORMA KAUKONEN'S "EMBRYONIC JOURNEY")

BRIGER: That was "Embryonic Journey" from the album "Wabash Avenue" that was released last year from my guest, Jorma Kaukonen. Jorma Kaukonen, welcome to FRESH AIR.

JORMA KAUKONEN: Hey, man. Thanks for having me.

BRIGER: So that was the first song you ever wrote?

KAUKONEN: Yeah. And I'm going to say it's sort of - it's a little self-inflating to say that I wrote that song, but it is the first song that I was - that I ever created, and it was one of those things that happened because, gosh, we had - this folky named Roger Perkins came through San Jose, where I was living at the time. And he played at The Offstage, where we all played back in those days. And he was the first person that I ever saw play in drop D, and he showed it to me, and I went, wow. And I went back to my little house in Santa Clara and started messing around with it. And my roommate at the time said, you know, that sounds like a song. Maybe you should do something with it. And ultimately, "Embryonic Journey" came out of it.

BRIGER: Right. When you say drop D, that means a particular kind of tuning, or you're changing the tuning on a guitar a little bit.

KAUKONEN: (Strumming guitar). I mean, that's a guitar in a straight tuning. (Tuning down, strumming guitar). The six string is down to D when you do that. It makes sort of a sonorous, hypnotic sound.

BRIGER: So that recording that we just heard happened in 1965. Your life was about to change drastically in just a few months, wasn't it?

KAUKONEN: It certainly was. And I remember - you know, Paul Kantner, who was in the Jefferson Airplane also - and he was a San Jose guy, and he had dropped out of Santa Clara.

BRIGER: Which is where you were going to school at the time.

KAUKONEN: Which is where I was going to school at the time. And there was a local music store in San Jose called the Benner Music Company, and Paul was teaching there, and he ultimately got me a job there, too. I mean, so much of that stuff, you know, that mutated into early Jefferson Airplane started at the Benner Music Company on Stevens Creek Boulevard in San Jose.

BRIGER: So you've said that the feeling of a guitar in your lap and your hand on the neck of the guitar has always surrounded you in a protective armor of tranquility. What do you mean by that?

KAUKONEN: Well, first of all, as we're talking here, I'm sitting with a guitar in my lap, even though I may or may not be playing. I mean, I...

BRIGER: I did ask you to bring it. You just didn't bring it as your emotional support guitar.

KAUKONEN: Well, it's my emotional support guitar, yeah. I was sort of a shy kid. And when I - but for some reason, when I started to play the guitar and learned a couple of songs to sing, I wasn't shy at all. And I would imagine that - I mean, I would just play in front of anybody under any circumstances. And to be honest with you, maybe I shouldn't have back then. I don't know, but I did. And so the performing thing, I just never felt uncomfortable with it. And so, once again, with a guitar in my lap and the possibility that I can hide behind playing it was always a great refuge.

BRIGER: Well, let's get back to the first time that you were really struck by the guitar. You had been living in Karachi, Pakistan. Your father had been the director of The Asia Foundation there.

KAUKONEN: Correct.

BRIGER: And you had returned back to the States, and were living again in D.C. And you went over to your friend's house, he hadn't seen it in a while, and he had an acoustic guitar.…
